coredata.dc:description: 1,2-Dichloroethane (DCE), a common chlorinated volatile organic compound (CVOC), poses serious environmental and health risks owing to its toxicity and persistence. Achieving its efficient and eco-friendly removal remains challenging, largely due to the inevitable formation of hazardous byproducts such as vinyl chloride (VC) and polychlorinated compounds during treatment. In this study, we demonstrate that the 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ catalyst exhibits outstanding performance in DCE oxidation, characterized by high activity, excellent stability, and remarkable water resistance, while effectively suppressing the generation of VC and polychlorinated byproducts. This superior behavior originates from synergistic interactions among multiple interfacial structures: CePO₄, ZrOₓ/CePO₄, Ru0/CePO₄, RuOₓ/CePO₄, and RuOₓ–ZrOₓ/CePO₄. DCE initially undergoes dehydrochlorination at acid–base sites on CePO₄ and ZrOₓ/CePO₄ interfaces; however, their limited redox capability restricts further oxidation of VC. Neighboring RuOₓ–ZrOₓ/CePO₄ interfaces facilitate rapid low-temperature oxidation and hydrolysis of VC, thereby preventing its accumulation and subsequent chlorination. Additionally, the RuOₓ–ZrOₓ/CePO₄ interfaces also promote direct hydrolytic dechlorination–oxidation of DCE. Electron transfer from CePO₄ to Ru species at Ru0/CePO₄ and RuOₓ/CePO₄ interfaces enhances CCl cleavage at Ce3+ sites and concurrently suppresses β‑hydrogen elimination at PO₄3− groups. The resulting electron-rich Ru sites at Ru0/CePO₄ and RuOₓ/CePO₄ interfaces enhance oxygen activation, thereby accelerating the deep oxidation of dechlorinated intermediates (e.g., *CH₂CH₂Cl) via both Mars–van Krevelen (MvK) and Langmuir–Hinshelwood (L–H) pathways. This multi-interface synergy establishes an efficient and environmentally benign catalytic framework for the complete elimination of DCE or other CVOCs, offering a promising strategy to minimize secondary pollution from chlorinated byproducts.

ce:section.ce:para: Chlorinated volatile organic compounds (CVOCs), such as 1,2-dichloroethane (DCE), vinyl chloride (VC), represent a class of hazardous air pollutants characterized by high toxicity, chemical stability, and potential carcinogenicity [1]. Their extensive use as industrial solvents, degreasing agents, and chemical intermediates has been contaminating the environment across multiple sectors, such as chemical plants, the chlor-alkali industry, pharmaceutical manufacturing, and package printing facilities [2]. Catalytic oxidation is regarded as one of the most promising technologies for DCE and other CVOCs removal, offering advantages including low operating temperatures, minimal energy consumption, and reduced secondary pollution [3]. The development of high-performance catalysts is crucial for advancing this technology. Redox-active transition metal oxides, such as CeO₂, Co₃O₄ and MnO2, exhibit strong oxygen activation capacity and high lattice oxygen mobility, while their weak-to-moderate Lewis (L) acid sites promote CCl bond cleavage, thereby facilitating the dechlorination, activation, and deep oxidation of CVOCs [4–8]. However, these L acid sites and oxygen vacancies can strongly adsorb chlorine (Cl) species during the long-term operation process, leading to Cl poisoning/accumulation and catalyst deactivation [9,10]. Moreover, their high redox activity enhances the Deacon reaction, resulting in significant Cl₂ generation. This Cl₂ can subsequently serve as a chlorinating agent, participating in electrophilic addition or substitution reactions with intermediates such as VC over surface M–Cl or M–OCl sites, thereby generating more toxic polychlorinated byproducts and causing secondary pollution [11,12]. In contrast, acidic transition metal oxides like WOₓ, MoOₓ, VOₓ and H-zeolite, possess abundant strong L and Brønsted (B) acid sites, which effectively catalyze the dehydrochlorination of DCE to form HCl and VC, thereby mitigating Cl poisoning. Nevertheless, their inherently poor redox properties impede the deep oxidation of VC and other dechlorinated intermediates, leading to the accumulation of these species in the reaction system and limiting their practical applicability [13–15].

Compared to conventional transition metal oxide catalysts, cerium phosphate (CePO₄) has attracted increasing interest as a promising catalytic material, exhibiting unique physicochemical properties and demonstrated potential in various reactions such as the water-gas shift and NOx reduction [16,17]. Its surface features a distinctive “acid–base pair” structure, composed of Ce3+ L acid sites and PO₄3− nucleophilic groups (alkaline sites). The Ce3+ sites are responsible for adsorbing CVOCs molecules and cleaving CCl bonds, while the PO₄3− groups promote the desorption of hydrogen species in the form of HCl [18], effectively mitigating surface Cl accumulation and poisoning. Moreover, the electron-modulating influence of PO₄3− on Ce3+ fine-tunes the chlorine adsorption strength, preserving adequate activity for molecular activation without allowing the formation of stable CeOCl or CeCl overlayers that irreversibly block active sites [19]. In addition, CePO₄ possesses a highly stable crystal structure with strong PO bonds, enabling it to maintain structural integrity under severe conditions—including high temperatures, Cl-rich atmospheres, and vapor stream—without undergoing phase transformation or collapse, thus ensuring long-term catalytic durability [20–22]. These attributes collectively make CePO₄ a highly suitable support or active component for catalytic combustion of CVOCs. However, similar to acidic transition metal oxides, the relatively poor redox capability of CePO₄ restricts the deep oxidation efficiency of reaction intermediates (especially the dehydrochlorination products, such as VC), necessitating further improvement of its overall catalytic performance. To overcome these limitations, constructing composite catalysts with multiple synergistic active sites on CePO₄ supports has emerged as an effective strategy for enhanced CVOCs degradation. For example, the incorporation of ZrOₓ improves the activation of water molecules and provides abundant surface hydroxyl groups, thereby facilitating rapid hydrolytic dechlorination pathways [23,24]. Meanwhile, the introduction of Ru species significantly enhances oxygen activation capacity and lattice oxygen mobility, while promoting the removal of surface chlorine via the Deacon reaction. When Ru and ZrOₓ are co-deposited on the CePO₄ surface, multiple interfacial structures are formed, such as Ru0/CePO₄, RuOₓ/CePO₄, ZrOₓ/CePO₄, and RuOₓ–ZrOₓ/CePO₄. This architecture enables a clear functional division: acidic sites mainly govern CVOCs adsorption-activation and hydrolytic dichlorination of chlorinated/dechlorinated products, while neighboring redox sites promote low-temperature oxidation and deep degradation of intermediates.

Based on this rationale, we successfully prepared a multifunctional 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ catalyst using sequential impregnation. Advanced characterization techniques including XRD, HAADF-STEM, XAS (EXAFS and XANES), XPS, Mott–Schottky plots, UV–Vis DRS, H₂-TPR, O₂-TPD, NH₃/CO₂-TPD, Py-FTIR, DFT calculation, and in situ DRIFTS were employed to systematically investigate its surface/bulk composition, surface-interface structure, interface electronic effect, etc. The catalytic performance was evaluated under various challenging conditions, including different oxygen concentrations, humidity levels, high reactant concentrations and electrostatic field (EF) condition during DCE oxidation. The results demonstrate outstanding activity, stability, water resistance, and effective suppression of VC and polychlorinated byproducts. These superior properties originate from synergistic catalytic mechanisms at the multiple interfaces. This work not only provides a novel catalyst design strategy for efficient CVOCs elimination, but also offers theoretical insights into structure-activity relationships in multicomponent catalytic systems.

The CePO₄ support was synthesized via a co-precipitation method. Specifically, 1.39 g of cerium(III) nitrate hexahydrate was dissolved in 200 mL of deionized water under continuous magnetic stirring at room temperature until a homogeneous colorless solution formed. Then, 200 mL of an aqueous solution containing 1.5 g of ammonium phosphate was slowly poured into the above cerium salt solution, yielding a white suspension. The resulting mixture was vigorously stirred for 0.5 h and subsequently aged at room temperature for 15 h. After decanting the supernatant, the precipitate was collected by centrifugation and washed five times alternately with deionized water and anhydrous ethanol to remove impurities. The washed precursor was dried in an oven at 80 °C, ground into powder, and finally calcined at 450 °C for 2 h in a muffle furnace under static air to obtain the final CePO₄ support.

All CePO₄-supported catalysts were prepared using the incipient wetness impregnation method. The 1% Ru-15% Zr/CePO₄ catalyst was synthesized through a sequential impregnation procedure: first, the 15% Zr/CePO₄ precursor was prepared, followed by the deposition of 1% Ru (where 1% and 15% represent the mass fractions of Ru and Zr species relative to the CePO₄ support, respectively). For comparison, a co-impregnated catalyst, denoted as 1% Ru-15% Zr/CePO₄-CI, was also prepared by impregnating 0.5 g of CePO₄ support with a mixed solution containing appropriate amounts of RuCl₃ and zirconium nitrate in a single step. Additionally, reference catalysts including 1% Ru/CePO₄, 15% Zr/CePO₄, and 1% Ru/ZrO₂ were prepared, where the ZrO₂ support was obtained by direct thermal decomposition of zirconium nitrate.

All impregnated samples were dried at 80 °C for 12 h and then calcined at 450 °C for 2 h in static air. ICP-OES analysis confirmed that the actual loadings of Ru and Zr in the 1% Ru-15% Zr/CePO₄ catalyst were 1.21 wt% and 14.43 wt%, respectively, showing close agreement with the theoretical values.

The synthesized catalysts were systematically characterized to determine their crystal structure, surface properties, and electronic state. Periodic density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed using the Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP), with detailed computational methods and parameters provided in the Supporting Information.

The catalytic oxidation of DCE was conducted in a continuous-flow fixed-bed quartz reactor with an internal diameter of 5 mm. To evaluate the proposed reaction mechanism under conditions that simulate real industrial environments (such as package printing industry), experiments were conducted using the following parameters: a gas flow of 20 mL min−1 O₂ and 80 mL min−1 N₂, with a low DCE concentration of 1000 mg m−3 and 1–5 vol% water vapor. Effluent gases were monitored using an online gas chromatograph equipped with a flame ionization detector and a CO₂ conversion furnace. Chlorinated byproducts such as vinyl chloride (VC), dichloroethylene, trichloroethylene (TCE), trichloroethane (TCA), perchloroethylene (PCE), and tetrachloroethane (TeCA) were identified and quantified. Detailed procedures for calculating DCE conversion and product concentration are provided in the Supporting Information. The catalytic oxidation of DCE under an electrostatic field (EF, 5 mA) was carried out in a fixed-bed flow reactor with a DC power supply, as shown in Scheme S1. The current was maintained at a low milliampere level (e.g., 5 mA) to minimize significant temperature rise caused by Joule heating.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Identification and interaction of multiphase interfaces
ce:section.ce:para: To identify the phase structure and assess the dispersion of active components on CePO4-based catalysts, XRD, Raman, and FT-IR analyses were performed. As shown in Fig. 1a, the diffraction peaks of pristine CePO₄ showed excellent agreement with the standard pattern for hexagonal CePO₄ (JCPDS No. 34–1380) [25]. The crystal structure of CePO₄ remained intact after the introduction of Zr or Ru species, either individually or via co-loading (1% Ru-15% Zr/CePO₄). No distinct diffraction peaks corresponding to Ru- or Zr-containing impurity phases were detected, indicating the high dispersion of both active species on the CePO₄ surface. This high dispersion was further confirmed by Raman spectroscopy (Fig. 1b), where no features attributable to crystalline Ru or Zr phases were observed. Notably, the introduction of Ru species induced a red shift in the PO vibrational bands, suggesting electron transfer from the CePO₄ support to Ru species, which modulated the electronic structure of surface PO₄3− units [26]. Similarly, ZrOₓ deposition enhanced the intensity of the 988 cm−1 Raman band, likely due to the electron-withdrawing effect of acidic Zr4+ species. Both Ru and Zr loadings caused broadening of the PO bands, indicating the introduction of local structural disorder.

Consistent with these findings, FT-IR spectra (Fig. 1c) showed a red shift in the ν₄ bending vibrations of PO₄3− after loading Zr or Ru, further confirming the strong interaction that weakens PO bonds and alters surface electron density [27]. For the 1% Ru/CePO₄ sample, a new peak at 1917 cm−1, attributed to CO adsorbed on metallic Ru0 species, confirmed the presence of Ru0 particles [28]. Morphological characterization by SEM (Fig. S1 and Fig. 1d) revealed that the 1% Ru-15% Zr/CePO₄ catalyst possessed an irregular block-like morphology with a rough surface composed of fine particles and some nanoneedles. SEM-EDX mapping (Fig. S2) confirmed the successful and relatively uniform loading of Ru and Zr species on the CePO₄ surface.

To directly visualize the nanoscale architecture and elemental distribution of the multiphase interfaces on 1% Ru-15% Zr/CePO4, HAADF-STEM and associated spectroscopy were employed. As shown in Fig. 2a–c, the 1% Ru-15% Zr/CePO₄ catalyst exhibited a complex composite structure. The support was identified as well-crystallized hexagonal CePO₄, with interplanar spacings (e.g., 0.611, 0.445, and 0.306 nm) matching the (1 0 0), (1 0 1), and (2 0 0) planes, respectively, consistent with XRD results [26,27]. Ru nanoclusters were clearly observed on the CePO₄ surface (white dashed area in Fig. 2b). Atomic-resolution imaging revealed lattice fringes of 0.215 nm, corresponding to the (0 0 2) plane of metallic Ru0, confirming the presence of single-crystalline Ru0 nanoclusters with exposed {0 0 1} facets [29–31]. Importantly, extensive amorphous regions were attributed to monolayer-dispersed ZrOₓ species (green dashed area, Fig. 2c). Adjacent to these ZrOₓ areas, RuOₓ nanoclusters with a lattice spacing of 0.224 nm (consistent with the (2 0 0) plane of RuO₂) were identified, indicating the formation of RuOₓ-ZrOₓ interfaces [32]. Local bright spots within the amorphous ZrOₓ regions further suggested the possible incorporation of Ru into the ZrOₓ matrix, hinting at Ru-O-Zr bonding (Fig. 2c, blue dashed area). Elemental mapping (Fig. 2d) corroborated this complex architecture, showing homogeneous distributions of Ce, O, P, and Zr, while Ru displayed a dual pattern of localized enrichment (corresponding to Ru/RuOₓ nanoclusters) and widespread dispersion (likely atomically dispersed species or Ru doped into ZrOₓ). These results provide direct evidence that the catalyst surface comprised a multifaceted interface system, including ZrOₓ/CePO₄, Ru0/CePO₄, RuOₓ/CePO₄, and RuOₓ-ZrOₓ/CePO₄, which collectively underpinned its synergistic functions in catalysis.

XPS analysis was employed to probe the surface electronic states and interfacial charge interactions within the catalysts. As summarized in Fig. 3 , analysis of the O 1 s, Ce 3d, P 2p, Zr 3d, and Ru 3p core levels provided direct evidence of strong electronic coupling between CePO4 support and active species. The O 1 s spectra (Fig. 3a,f) revealed that Ru loading, especially in the 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ composite, significantly increased the proportion of surface-adsorbed oxygen (OII). This was attributed to partial incorporation of Ru species into the ZrOₓ lattice (STEM results), which increased the surface oxygen vacancies in ZrOₓ species [33]. Concomitantly, the binding energies of lattice oxygen (OI), Ce3+, and P5+ all shifted to higher values upon the introduction of Zr or Ru species (Fig. 3a-c). These synchronized shifts collectively point to electron transfer from the CePO₄ support to the surface-loaded ZrOₓ and RuOₓ species, which modulates the electron density and acid-base properties of the surface Ce3+ and PO₄3− sites [33–35]. Further evidence comes from the Zr and Ru states. The Zr 3d spectra showed an increased proportion of Zr3+ in the 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ catalyst (Fig. 3d,f), further suggesting Ru incorporation promoted the formation of oxygen vacancies in the ZrOₓ phase [24,36]. Moreover, the Zr 3d binding energies in both 15% Zr/CePO₄ and 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ shift toward lower values relative to those in 1% Ru/ZrO₂ (Fig. 3d), further confirming that the loaded ZrOₓ species exist as coordinatively unsaturated nanoclusters, consistent with the STEM observations. The Ru 3p spectra provided a clear contrast: while Ru existed primarily as higher-valent Ru4+/Ru3+ in 1% Ru/ZrO₂, a significant metallic Ru0 component (18.35%) was identified in 1% Ru/CePO₄ (Fig. 3e,f). This demonstrates the unique role of CePO₄ as an electron donor, stabilizing lower-valence Ru species [37,38]. In the 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ catalyst, the presence of both Ru0 and lower Ru 3p binding energies confirms that a portion of Ru directly interacts with the electron-donating CePO₄ support, in addition to Ru species likely incorporated into the ZrOₓ matrix. Thus, XPS analysis conclusively identified electron transfer from CePO₄ to Ru and Zr species as a key interfacial effect, which enriched the electron density of Ru sites (facilitating O₂ activation) and tailors the surface acidity/basicity of CePO₄ (promoting CCl cleavage).

To elucidate the interfacial electronic structure and charge transfer behavior, a combination of spectroscopic and electrochemical characterizations was performed. First, UV–Vis DRS (Fig. 4a) revealed that introducing Ru and Zr species enhanced the light absorption of CePO₄, with Ru-modified catalysts showing the most significant improvement. The observed bandgap narrowing, particularly for 1% Ru/CePO₄, was attributed to the strong metal-support interaction and the localized surface plasmon resonance of metallic Ru0 nanoparticles [39,40]. Mott-Schottky analysis (Fig. 4b) further probed the energy level alignment. The more negative flat-band potential of 1% Ru/CePO₄ (−0.43 V) versus 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ (−0.31 V) indicated that its conduction band minimum was better positioned relative to the O₂/O₂− redox potential (−0.33 V), providing a stronger thermodynamic driving force for electron transfer to O₂ and superior oxygen activation capability at the Ru0/CePO₄ interface [41]. Critically, transient photocurrent tests (Fig. 4c) provided direct dynamic evidence for the promoted charge separation and transfer. In the dark, only Ru-containing catalysts exhibited noticeable current, with the 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ composite showing the strongest response, underscoring Ru's key role and the synergy with Zr in facilitating interfacial electron transport. Under illumination, all catalysts generated photocurrent, and the 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ again showed the highest response, further confirming the most efficient charge transfer capability between CePO4 support and RuZr co existing composite interface [29,30]. Finally, CO adsorption IR spectroscopy (Fig. 4f) was employed to identify the dispersion states of Ru species. After pre-reduction, surface Ru species were predominantly in reduced forms (Ru0 or Ruδ+, δ+ < 4). As shown in Fig. 4f, no adsorbed CO was detected on 15% Zr/CePO₄, whereas 1% Ru/ZrO₂ exhibited a single band at 1885 cm−1, characteristic of bridge-bonded CO on Ru0 sites associated with ZrOₓ. In contrast, 1% Ru/CePO₄ showed two distinct bands at 2028 and 2091 cm−1, assigned to linearly adsorbed CO on partially reduced Ruδ+ and metallic Ru0 sites, respectively [42]. For the composite catalyst 1% Ru–15% ZrOₓ/CePO₄, the spectrum revealed multiple features: a band at 1892 cm−1 corresponding to Ru0 anchored on the ZrOₓ phase; two bands red-shifted relative to those on 1% Ru/CePO₄, indicating electronic perturbation of Ru sites by adjacent ZrOₓ; and a weak band near 2065 cm−1 attributed to Ruδ+ species situated at the ZrOₓ/CePO₄ interface [42]. Collectively, these results paint a coherent picture: the catalyst of 1% Ru–15% ZrOₓ/CePO₄ features a multifaceted interface architecture (Ru0/CePO₄, RuOₓ/CePO₄, RuOx–ZrOₓ/CePO₄). The strong electronic interactions within this architecture, evidenced by modulated band structures, enhanced charge transfer, and diverse Ru anchoring sites, synergistically tailor the surface properties for optimal DCE oxidation.

To gain atomic-scale insights into the interfacial bonding and local structure of the active species, XAS was performed on the 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ catalyst. The absorption edge position between Zr foil and ZrO₂ (Fig. S3a) confirmed the presence of low-valent Zr3+, consistent with XPS. The EXAFS spectrum (Fig. S3b) showed a ZrO first-shell peak at ∼1.62 Å, which was longer and less intense than that in crystalline ZrO₂ (∼1.58 Å), indicating a reduced coordination number and elongated bonds characteristic of small, disordered ZrOₓ nanoclusters. The concomitant weakening and shift of the ZrZr scattering peak further supported this nanostructured model. Crucially, wavelet transform analysis (Fig. S3c–e) demonstrated a pronounced weakening and a shift to lower k/R values for both ZrO and ZrZr signals compared to pure ZrO₂. This directly evidenced the structural perturbation caused by Ru incorporation [43,44], suggesting the formation of RuOZr mixed oxide units at the interface, which promoted oxygen vacancy formation. Ru K-edge XAS analysis (Fig. 5a–e) complemented this picture by elucidating the state of Ru. The edge position between Ru0 and RuO₂ (Fig. 5a) indicated a mixed valence state between 0 and +4 [43]. EXAFS (Fig. 5b) showed dominant RuO scattering (∼1.50 Å) and a much weaker RuRu contribution (∼2.45 Å) [44], signifying that Ru existed primarily as oxidized species (RuOₓ) or within a RuOZr network, with only a minor fraction as metallic Ru0 nanoclusters. The elongated RuO bond and lower FT peak intensity versus crystalline RuO₂ were attributed to Ru integration into the amorphous ZrOₓ lattice, causing local distortion and facilitating oxygen mobility. Wavelet transform analysis (Fig. 5c–e) visually corroborated the dominance of a broad RuO coordination environment alongside a faint RuRu signal. XAS analysis conclusively identifies the atomic-scale synergy at the interface: ZrOₓ exists as highly dispersed, low-crystallinity nanoclusters, while Ru species were partially incorporated into this matrix, forming RuOZr bridging structures. This configuration, rich in oxygen vacancies and structural disorder, was pivotal for enhanced oxygen migration and activation. These findings, fully consistent with STEM, XPS, and CO-IR results, solidify the understanding that coexisting interfaces (Ru0/CePO₄, RuOₓ/CePO₄, RuOₓ–ZrOₓ/CePO₄) synergistically govern the efficient catalytic oxidation of DCE.

To comprehensively evaluate the critical surface and bulk properties governing catalytic performance, the redox behavior, oxygen vacancy concentration, and acid-base characteristics of the catalysts were systematically probed. H₂-TPR and O₂-TPD analyses were first conducted to assess reducibility and oxygen mobility (Fig. 6a,b). Pure CePO₄ showed inert redox nature without the obvious peaks in its H₂-TPR and O₂-TPD profiles. The introduction of 15% ZrOₓ induced only a broad H₂ consumption and O₂ desorption above 500 °C (Fig. 6a,b), indicating a marginal improvement. In stark contrast, 1% Ru/CePO₄ exhibited significant low-temperature reduction, with peaks at 115 °C and 171 °C attributed to the reduction of oxygen adsorbed on Ru0 sites and surface oxygen vacancies of RuOₓ clusters, respectively (Fig. 6a). The O₂-TPD profile for 1% Ru/CePO₄ showed a corresponding adsorbed oxygen desorption peak at 82 °C (Fig. 6b). The H₂-TPR profile of 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ featured a broad reduction peak at 174 °C and a distinct new peak at 372 °C (Fig. 6a). This higher-temperature peak was assigned to the reduction of lattice oxygen within Ru–O–Zr interfacial structures formed by Ru incorporation into the ZrOₓ framework. Accordingly, O₂-TPD revealed lattice oxygen release from this structure at 508 °C (Fig. 6b). These findings demonstrate that Ru not only provides low-temperature redox sites but, when integrated with ZrOₓ, creates a unique interface that significantly enhances lattice oxygen mobility. This conclusion was further corroborated by EPR spectroscopy, where the 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ sample exhibited the most intense signal for oxygen vacancies (g = 2.003, Fig. 6c) [6].

The surface acidity of these catalysts was derived from NH₃-TPD and Py-FTIR, as shown in Fig. 6d,e. Pure CePO₄ contained both moderate-acid (100–300 °C) and strong-acid (300–500 °C) sites (Fig. 6d). Py-FTIR identified co-existing Lewis (L, Ce3+) and Brønsted (B, from POH/CeOH) acid sites on CePO4 (Fig. 6e), evidenced by a strong band at 1483 cm−1 (L + B) [45]. Loading 15% ZrOₓ significantly increased the NH₃ desorption intensity from moderate-acid sites and enhanced the L acid signal at 1443 cm−1 in Py-FTIR (Fig. 6d,e), which was attributed to the introduction of stronger L acid sites from surface Zr4+. ZrOH groups also contributed a small number of B acid sites (1540 cm−1) (Fig. 6e). For 1% Ru/CePO₄, the absence of the B acid signal at 1540 cm−1 suggested Ru species reacted with and consumed original B acid sites (e.g., POH) (Fig. 6e). Concurrently, increased L acid intensity in Py-FTIR and slightly enhanced NH₃ desorption indicated that Ru4+/Ru3+ species provided additional L acid sites (Fig. 6d,e). Critically, in the 1% Ru-15% Zr/CePO₄ composite, the strong L acidity and weak B acidity from ZrOₓ was preserved (Fig. 6e). A distinct new peak of NH₃ desorption on strong-acid sites appeared at 359 °C (Fig. 6d). This peak was assigned to NH₃ adsorption on the oxygen vacancies of Ru-modified ZrOₓ nanoclusters, a finding consistent with the reduction peak of surface lattice oxygen at 372 °C in H₂-TPR (Fig. 6a). This confirms that Ru incorporation not only enhances L acidity but also creates vacancy-associated acid sites linked to improved redox properties.

The surface basicity, probed by CO₂-TPD (Fig. 6f), was also modulated. The surfaces of CePO₄ and 15% Zr/CePO₄ were dominated by strong basic sites (CO₂ desorption >300 °C), likely originating from deprotonated species like PO− or ZrO− [19,46], which could facilitate dehydrogenation. For 1% Ru/CePO₄, the introduction of Ru species reduced the intensity of these strong basic sites while increasing desorption in the moderate-strength region (100–300 °C). This electronic modulation by Ru, which lowers the electron density of basic sites like PO₄3− (as indicated by XPS), likely suppresses their nucleophilicity, thereby inhibiting the β-H elimination step responsible for VC formation during DCE activation. In the 1% Ru-15% Zr/CePO₄ catalyst, a synergistic interaction between ZrOₓ and RuOₓ resulted in a moderate CO₂ desorption intensity, achieving an optimal balance of basicity between its single-modified counterparts. The sequential introduction of Zr and Ru engineered an optimal and synergistic surface chemical environment. The composite catalyst maintains strong L acidity for CCl cleavage, introduces unique acid sites associated with oxygen vacancies, and tailors the basicity to suppress undesirable side reactions. This optimized acid-base property, integrated with enhanced redox functionality, underpins its superior performance in the efficient dechlorination and deep oxidation of DCE.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Influence of multiphase interface synergy on performance
ce:section.ce:para: To elucidate the role of these interfaces in DCE activation and oxidation, we comparatively evaluated the catalytic performance of 1% Ru/ZrO2, CePO4, 1% Ru/CePO₄, 15% Zr/CePO₄, and 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ catalysts (Fig. 7a). Loading 15 wt% Zr onto CePO₄ (15% Zr/CePO₄) significantly reduced the T₉₀ from 329 °C to 271 °C, attributable to the increased surface acidity promoting DCE activation and dechlorination (as confirmed by NH₃-TPD/Py-FTIR). In contrast, loading 1 wt% Ru alone (1% Ru/CePO₄) only lowered T₉₀ to 312 °C. The 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ composite catalyst achieved the best performance, with the lowest T₉₀ of 260 °C, highlighting a synergistic effect. Analysis of COₓ products (Fig. 7b) revealed that while CePO₄ and 15% Zr/CePO₄ maintained high CO levels (>275 °C) with low CO₂ yield—indicating poor deep oxidation ability—the Ru-containing catalysts showed a distinct, low-temperature “volcano” profile for CO. The 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ catalyst, in particular, limited maximum CO to <100 ppm, achieved complete CO elimination before 250 °C, and yielded a CO₂ concentration near the theoretical 500 ppm. This confirms that Ru species critically enhance redox properties, and their combination with Zr synergistically drives the reaction toward complete oxidation.

Fig. 7c,d showed the temperature-dependent concentration profiles of chlorinated by-products over different catalysts. The formation of polychlorinated compounds during DCE combustion was governed by sequential chlorination and dechlorination of the primary dechlorination product, VC. Thus, suppressing VC generation is the most effective strategy for controlling polychlorinated by-products at source. Both CePO₄ and 15% Zr/CePO₄ produced VC as the dominant byproduct, with peak concentrations exceeding 30 ppm (Fig. 7c), though ZrOₓ incorporation slightly lowered and shifted this peak. Notably, no polychlorinated compounds such as TCA, PCE, or TeCA were detected over these two catalysts (Fig. 7d). Similarly, neither PCE nor TeCA was observed over 1% Ru/CePO₄ or 1% Ru-15% Zr/CePO₄ (Fig. 7d). Only trace amounts of TCA below 0.5 ppm, considered negligible, were detected in the temperature range of 150–270 °C for these two Ru-modified catalysts (Fig. 7d). These results demonstrated that the CePO₄ support effectively suppressed the formation of polychlorinated by-products. The introduction of Ru species dramatically inhibited VC formation, suppressing its peak below 5 ppm for 1% Ru/CePO₄ and nearly eliminating it for the 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ composite ( Fig. 7c). This highlighted the crucial role of Ru species in inhibiting VC formation and further revealed that the co-loading of Ru and Zr species synergistically enhanced this inhibitory effect. Other dechlorinated intermediates (dichloroethylene, TCE) appeared at very low concentrations (<2 ppm) (Fig. 7d). The addition of ZrOₓ improved DCE dehydrochlorination, lowering the onset temperature for dechlorinated product formation to 150–250 °C, whereas Ru promoted their low-temperature conversion, leading to complete elimination below 275 °C with the composite catalyst (Fig. 7d).

A critical comparison with 1% Ru/ZrO₂ revealed the unique protective role of the CePO₄ support. The 1% Ru/ZrO₂ catalyst suffered significant activity loss at 175–250 °C (Fig. 7a) and produced markedly more TCA (Fig. 7d), indicative of severe Cl poisoning via surface M–Cl/M–OCl species and Cl₂-mediated re-chlorination [9]. In stark contrast, the CePO₄-supported Ru catalysts (1% Ru/CePO₄ and 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄) showed no significant activity drop and generated far less VC and TCA (Fig. 7a,c,d). The CePO₄ support, through its acid-base pairs, facilitated efficient Cl removal as HCl, preventing the Cl₂ cycle responsible for polychlorinated byproduct formation. The trace TCA observed on the Ru/CePO₄ and 1% Ru-15% Zr/CePO₄ catalysts was likely linked to isolated RuOₓ or RuOₓ–ZrOₓ sites, but its concentration was orders of magnitude lower than on Ru/ZrO₂ (Fig. 7d). The catalytic evaluation confirmed that the 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ catalyst uniquely combines high activity (T₉₀ = 260 °C), complete oxidation selectivity, and exceptional suppression of toxic byproducts like VC. This superior performance stems from a synergistic effect between the CePO₄ support and the Ru/Zr active sites. This integrated functionality distinguished it from conventional oxide catalysts, as further emphasized by its favorable comparison with state-of-the-art materials (Table S1).

A systematic optimization of catalyst composition and preparation method was conducted to establish the structure-activity relationships governing DCE oxidation performance. This study pinpointed the optimal Zr and Ru loadings, the superior sequential impregnation method, and the advantage of Ru over Pt, collectively justifying the design of the 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ catalyst. The influence of Zr loading (x% Zr/CePO₄, x = 5, 10, 15, 20) was first investigated (Fig. S4 and S5). Increasing Zr content beyond 5% did not markedly improve DCE conversion or alter the VC formation profile, indicating that ZrOₓ species achieved a monolayer dispersion on the CePO₄ surface at moderate loadings, consistent with prior reports [47]. Higher Zr loadings did, however, shifted the formation of dechlorinated intermediates (dichloroethylene, TCE) to lower temperatures and increase their peak concentrations (Fig. S5a,b), due to the increased density of acid sites promoting further dechlorination.

The subsequent introduction of 1% Ru onto these Zr-loaded supports revealed a clear optimum. The 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ catalyst demonstrated the best high-temperature activity (>220 °C, Fig. 8a), the most pronounced shift of VC and other intermediates to lower temperatures (Figs. 8b, S6a–c), and the highest CO₂ yield (Fig. S6d). This optimal performance was attributed to the ideal monolayer dispersion at 15% Zr loading. This structure maximizes the active ZrOₓ/CePO₄ interfaces for DCE activation while allowing the subsequently deposited Ru to optimally distribute, forming abundant RuOₓ–ZrOₓ/CePO₄ interfaces for intermediate oxidation and sufficient Ru0/CePO₄ sites for oxygen activation. In contrast, lower Zr loadings (5%, 10%) leaded to incomplete coverage, causing most Ru to deposit directly on CePO₄ and failed to form the critical RuOₓ–ZrOₓ interfaces, resulting in intermediate accumulation. Excessively high Zr loading (20%) caused ZrOₓ aggregation into less active crystalline ZrO₂, where deposited Ru formed Ru/ZrO₂-like interfaces prone to Cl poisoning (Fig. 7a,d), weakening the beneficial Ru-CePO₄ interaction.

With the optimal 15% Zr support, the Ru loading was varied (x% Ru-15% Zr/CePO₄, x = 0.5–2). Increasing Ru content did not significantly boost DCE conversion (Fig. 8c), as Ru provided weaker acidity than ZrOₓ. However, raising the loading from 0.5% to 1% effectively decreased the peak concentrations of VC, dichloroethylene, TCE, and TCA, shifting their profiles to lower temperatures (Fig. 8d, S7a-c), while also lowering CO and increasing CO₂ yield (Fig. S7e,f). This improvement stemmed from enhanced O₂ activation and Cl desorption by Ru species. Crucially, excessive Ru loading (2%) was detrimental, leading to the appearance of PCE, higher concentrations of other chlorinated by-products, and a lower final CO₂ yield (Fig. S7). This was attributed to excessive Cl₂ generation via the promoted Deacon reaction, which facilitates the re-chlorination of reaction intermediates [45].

The preparation sequence critically affected catalyst structure. The sequentially impregnated catalyst (1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄) consistently outperformed its co-impregnated counterpart (1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄-CI), showing higher activity above 230 °C, higher CO₂ yield, and lower CO production (Fig. 8e, S8e,f). Under dry conditions, the co-impregnated catalyst yielded a much higher VC peak (>30 ppm), higher levels of other dechlorinated products, and even trace TeCA (Fig. 8f, S8a,b,d). Water vapor mitigated byproduct formation for both. These differences confirm that sequential impregnation is essential for forming the cooperative RuOₓ–ZrOₓ/CePO₄ and RuOₓ/CePO₄ interfaces that enable efficient dechlorination-oxidation [47]. Replacing Ru with an equivalent amount of Pt (1% Pt–15% Zr/CePO₄) resulted in inferior activity and higher yields of VC (>25 ppm), dichloroethylene, TCE, and trace PCE (Fig. 8g,h, S9a-c). Pt is known to promote CC bond activation in VC, leading to further HCl/Cl₂ addition and dechlorination [48]. Furthermore, comparing supports, 15% Zr/CePO₄ outperformed 15% Ce/CePO₄ (Fig. 8g,h), as supported CeOₓ is prone to forming chlorinated CeOClₓ species that poison the surface, and its weaker acidity is less effective for dehydrochlorination [49]. The systematic optimization validates the design principles: a 15% Zr loading achieves an ideal monolayer for maximizing interfaces; a 1% Ru loading balances oxidation enhancement with minimal harmful Cl₂ production; a sequential impregnation method is crucial for forming synergistic interfacial structures; and Ru is superior to Pt for this reaction system. This rigorous process culminated in the high-performance 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ catalyst.

To assess the catalyst's robustness and interfacial function under complex, realistic conditions, its performance was evaluated under humid atmospheres, in dedicated VC combustion tests, and with an applied electric field (EF). The impact of water vapor, a common component in industrial exhaust, was first examined. The introduction of 3 vol% H₂O decreased the activity of all CePO₄-based catalysts (Fig. 9a,b), with the most pronounced T₉₀ increase for CePO₄ and 1% Ru/CePO₄ due to competitive adsorption at L acid sites. However, a key benefit was the dramatic suppression of VC; its peak concentration was significantly reduced under humidity, nearly eliminated over the Ru-containing catalysts (Fig. 9a,c). For the optimal 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ catalyst, performance was tested across 1–5 vol% H₂O (Fig. S10). While activity and CO₂ yield gradually declined with increasing humidity—owing to competitive adsorption—the catalyst maintained a low T₉₀ of 303 °C even at 5 vol% H₂O, significantly outperforming all references (Fig. 9b, S10a). This demonstrates superior water tolerance, attributed to the synergistic multiphase interfaces where ZrOₓ aids water activation and Ru sites maintain redox function. Notably, while 1% Ru/ZrO₂ showed improved conversion under humidity, it suffered from increased TCA formation (Fig. S11c), highlighting the CePO₄ support's unique role in preventing chlorine-mediated secondary pollution.

To pinpoint the origin of VC suppression, direct VC combustion tests were conducted (Fig. 9d). The activity trend (1% Ru/ZrO₂ > 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ > 1% Ru/CePO₄ > > CePO₄ ≈ 15% Zr/CePO₄) and corresponding COₓ yields (Fig. 9e) clearly identified RuOₓ-based sites as the primary centers for VC activation and deep oxidation. The exceptionally high activity of 1% Ru/ZrO₂ confirmed the intrinsic VC oxidation capability of RuOₓ-ZrOₓ interfaces. Therefore, the effective suppression of VC during DCE oxidation over 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ is ascribed to the rapid capture and oxidation of VC intermediates at the adjacent RuOₓ–ZrOₓ/CePO₄ interfaces, preventing their accumulation and subsequent chlorination.

To further probe the interfacial charge dynamics and catalytic efficiency, reactions were conducted under a 5 mA electrostatic field (EF) [50]. The EF dramatically boosted activity, with all CePO₄-based catalysts achieving >95% DCE conversion below 150 °C (Fig. 9f). The 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ composite again exhibited exceptional performance, achieving full conversion at 100–150 °C and near-theoretical CO₂ yield (Fig. 9f, S12c). Under the EF, while pure CePO₄ and 15% Zr/CePO₄ still produced significant VC at low temperatures (100–250 °C) due to enhanced dehydrochlorination, the composite catalyst effectively suppressed VC and other chlorinated byproducts (Fig. 9f, S12a,b,d). This underscores that the EF primarily accelerates existing pathways; it enhances the dehydrochlorination function of acid-base sites but also promotes lattice oxygen migration at the RuOₓ/ZrOₓ interface, thereby drastically improving the dechlorination-oxidation efficiency of the composite. Even in a humid EF atmosphere, the 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ maintained stable, complete conversion at 100–150 °C, demonstrating its robust and efficient interfacial synergy. In summary, rigorous testing under challenging conditions confirmed the multifunctional superiority of the 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ catalyst. It exhibits remarkable water tolerance and near-complete VC suppression due to synergistic interfacial action, with the RuOₓ–ZrOₓ/CePO₄ interface identified as the key site for VC oxidation.

To elucidate the fundamental activation pathways and assess robustness under demanding, variable conditions, the catalytic performance was further investigated across anaerobic, humid, high‑oxygen, and high-concentration DCE environments. Under oxygen-free atmosphere (Fig. 10a), DCE conversion relied solely on surface-mediated dechlorination and lattice oxygen oxidation. The 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ catalyst exhibited the highest conversion, confirming the primary role of ZrOₓ species in DCE activation. Concurrently, it produced the highest concentration of VC in the 220–350 °C range, due to its optimal combination of acid sites (Zr4+, Ce3+, Zr–OH) for dechlorination and active species (Ru–O–Zr lattice oxygen, PO₄3−) for β-H elimination. Above 250 °C, VC and other dechlorinated intermediates (dichloroethylene, TCE) decreased sharply over this catalyst, accompanied by a measurable COₓ yield (Fig. S13), indicating their consumption by the lattice oxygen from RuOₓ–ZrOₓ interfacial sites. In contrast, 1% Ru/CePO₄ showed lower activity and less VC at high temperatures (>325 °C), suggesting Ru modification altered the electronic structure of CePO₄, slightly inhibiting its inherent dechlorination function (Fig. 10a). The stark contrast between high VC yield under anaerobic conditions and its near absence under aerobic oxidation (Fig. 7c) underscores the indispensable role of Ru species in activating gas-phase O₂ for VC suppression. Introducing 3 vol% H₂O under anaerobic conditions enhanced the activity of catalysts containing ZrOₓ (1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄, 15% Zr/CePO₄, 1% Ru/ZrO₂), lowering their T₉₀ compared to those in N₂ atmosphere (Fig. 10a,b). This is attributed to ZrOₓ-facilitated hydrolysis, converting H₂O into active hydroxyls that promote DCE hydrolysis-dechlorination. For 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄, humid conditions also lowered the peak VC concentration and facilitated its degradation above 300 °C (Fig. 10b), suggesting a hydrolytic-oxidative pathway at the RuOₓ–ZrOₓ interface. At elevated temperatures above 300 °C, the introduction of water vapor increased the COₓ yield over the Ru-containing catalysts, particularly over 1% Ru-15% Zr/CePO₄ and 1% Ru/ZrO₂ (Fig. S13d and Fig. S14d). This was likely due to a cleaning effect on surface-deposited species. Consequently, compared to dry anaerobic conditions, byproducts such as dichloroethylene, TCE, and PCE were more readily suppressed or completely degraded at high temperatures in the presence of water vapor over these catalysts (Fig. S13a–c and Fig. S14a–c).

Under a high oxygen concentration (50% O₂, Fig. 10c), catalysts like CePO₄, 1% Ru/CePO₄ and 1% Ru/ZrO2 suffered activity loss primarily due to competitive adsorption between O₂ and DCE molecules at active sites. The 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ catalyst, however, showed slightly improved conversion and complete VC suppression. This is attributed to its compartmentalized adsorption-activation scheme: O₂ preferentially activates at RuOₓ–ZrOₓ (or Ru0) redox sites, while DCE adsorbs and activates at ZrOₓ/CePO₄ acid-base sites. This cooperative mechanism alleviated the competitive adsorption effect induced by variations in reactant concentration, thereby enhancing activity/CO2 production under high oxygen conditions and effectively suppressing byproduct formation (Fig. S15). For 1% Ru/ZrO2, high O₂ concentration promoted the Deacon reaction, increasing Cl₂ production that facilitated further chlorination and led to higher concentrations of chlorinated byproducts such as TCA (Fig. S15d). At a high DCE concentration (3000 mg·m−3, Fig. 10d), the degradation activity of CePO₄ and 1% Ru/CePO₄ decreased significantly, the latter more severely, due to intermediate accumulation hindering O₂ activation. Conversely, 1% Ru/ZrO₂ showed improved activity (lower T₉₀) as high DCE concentration accelerated the MvK redox cycle. Remarkably, the 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ catalyst maintained optimal performance, with high CO₂ yield and rapid elimination of VC and other byproducts below 300 °C (Fig. S16). This demonstrates the superior synergistic adsorption-activation capability across its multifunctional interfaces, which efficiently manages high reactant loads without deactivation or selectivity loss.

To evaluate the practical durability and resistance to deactivation under realistic, fluctuating conditions, rigorous long-term and water vapor cycling stability tests were performed (Fig. 11a–h). During extended operation (≥3 h), the performance of pure CePO₄ gradually declined, accompanied by increased VC formation (Fig. 11a). Post-reaction XPS analysis (Fig. S17a, c) showed a positive shift in the binding energies of surface PO₄3− lattice oxygen (OI), Ce3+ 3d, and P5+ 2p for CePO₄, along with the strongest Cl 2p signal. This indicated significant Cl accumulation, primarily on Ce3+ sites, which poisoned active centers, hindered deep oxidation of intermediates like VC, dichloroethylene, and TCE, and led to a decreasing COₓ yield over time (Fig. S19a,b). However, XRD patterns of these CePO4-based catalysts after stability tests confirmed the bulk structure remained stable (Fig. S18). The introduction of either Zr or Ru species reduced surface Cl retention, with ZrOₓ-containing catalysts showing the most pronounced reduction in Cl signal (Fig. S17c). In contrast to CePO₄, the 15% Zr/CePO₄ catalyst exhibited negative XPS shifts for OI and P5+ after testing (Fig. S17a), suggesting surface electronic restructuring. However, its DCE conversion and COₓ yield still decreased after 3 h (Fig. 11b and Fig. S19c), likely due to coke accumulation driven by its strong acidity coupled with insufficient redox properties.

Remarkably, the Ru-containing catalysts displayed stable or even improving activity with time (Fig. 11c,d). For 1% Ru/CePO₄ and particularly 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄, post-reaction XPS (Fig. S17b and Fig. 3f) confirmed a decrease in metallic Ru0 and an increase in Ru3+, indicating the in-situ formation of highly dispersed, active RuOₓ clusters. These species served as efficient oxidation centers, and meanwhile promoted the Deacon reaction, enabling continuous Cl removal and active site regeneration. The reaction atmosphere also promoted oxygen vacancy formation on RuOₓ–ZrOₓ sites, as evidenced by slightly increased Zr3+ content (Fig. S17b and Fig. 3f). This synergistic effect led to the nearly complete suppression of chlorinated byproducts (VC, dichloroethylene, TCE) after 3 h and maintained high COₓ yields (Fig. 11c,d and Fig. S19e–h).

Periodic water vapor switching tests further probed stability under humidity fluctuations (Fig. 11e–h). For CePO₄, activity and COₓ yield dropped during “H₂O on” stages (3–6, 9–12, 16–18 h) due to competitive adsorption, and VC increased in subsequent dry periods (Fig. 11e and Fig. S20a). Performance of CePO4 failed to recover fully after multiple switching cycles, indicating irreversible hydrothermal deactivation (Fig. 11e and Fig. S20a). The 15% Zr/CePO₄ catalyst recovered its baseline activity after cycles (Fig. 11f), confirming the water-tolerant nature of ZrOₓ. However, the first wet-dry transition increased the formation of VC, dichloroethylene, and TCE while lowering COₓ yield (Fig. 11f, S20c,d). This occurred because water dissociation on ZrOₓ promoted dehydrochlorination, but its limited redox capability under subsequent dry conditions hindered deep oxidation. Notably, hydroxyl occupation of ZrOₓ surface oxygen vacancies after water treatment weakened lattice oxygen mobility, increasing partial oxidation product accumulation (Fig. S20d). The 1% Ru/CePO₄ catalyst showed decreased activity in later “H₂O on” stages but exhibited lower VC formation and higher COₓ selectivity in subsequent dry periods after the first cycle (Fig. 11g, S20e), suggesting water-induced transformation of Ru species enhanced its oxidation function. Most impressively, the 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ composite demonstrated exceptional robustness and adaptive optimization. Its activity remained nearly identical across all three “H₂O on” stages. In later “H₂O off” stages, DCE conversion remained higher than initial levels, VC concentration continuously decreased, and COₓ yield was stable under both wet and dry conditions (Fig. 11h, S20g). Concentrations of dichloroethylene and TCE also decreased in later cycles (Fig. S20h). These results indicate that water vapor cycling induced a beneficial reconstruction and optimization of surface active sites, particularly at the RuOₓ–ZrOₓ/CePO₄ interface, enhancing both water activation and the synergistic “activation-oxidation” cycle for DCE and its intermediates.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Synergistic mechanism of DCE degradation over multiphase interfaces
ce:section.ce:para: To elucidate the surface reaction pathways and identify the critical roles of different active sites, in situ DRIFTS was employed to monitor the adsorption and oxidation of DCE over CePO₄-based catalysts. The results provide direct spectroscopic evidence for the adsorption configurations, intermediate evolution, and reveal how Ru modification alters the reaction mechanism to suppress VC formation. The in situ DRIFTS spectra of DCE over CePO₄ were shown in Fig. 12a,b. At 50 °C, the consumption of Ce–OH groups (negative peaks at 3668 and 3715 cm−1) and the appearance of vibrational signals for adsorbed DCE –CH₂– stretching (2970 cm−1), bending (1451 and 1431 cm−1), and CCl stretching (725 cm−1) indicated that DCE could be adsorbed and activated even at low temperatures (Fig. 12a and Fig. S21) [47,51]. Although hydroxyl sites participated in initial adsorption, the surface was dominated by L acid sites (Ce3+), which served as the primary centers for CCl bond cleavage. Upon heating above 300 °C under oxygen (Fig. 12b), weak features of carboxylate/carbonate species (ν(C=O) at 1712 cm−1, ν(COO−) at 1582 cm−1, ν(CO₃2−) at 1458 cm−1) and CO₂ were detected [51,52]. These originated from the further oxidation of dechlorinated *CH₂CH₂Cl intermediates by activated PO₄3− groups. However, their low intensity reflected the poor redox capability of CePO₄, causing the reaction to favor a pathway where activated PO₄3− abstracted β‑hydrogens, leading to VC formation (Fig. 7c). The absence of characteristic VC signals in the DRIFTS spectra suggested that once formed, VC did not re-adsorb or undergo further activation on CePO₄, consistent with its poor VC combustion activity (Fig. 9d).

The introduction of Ru species fundamentally changed the surface process, as seen in the DRIFTS spectra for 1% Ru/CePO₄ (Fig. 12c,d). Under anaerobic conditions, more intense –CH₂– bending vibrations (1451 and 1431 cm−1) were observed at 50–200 °C compared to CePO₄, indicating enhanced DCE adsorption/activation. Differential charge density analysis (Fig. 12e and Fig. S22) quantified that 0.12 electrons transferred from CePO₄ to the supported RuOₓ nanoclusters [53]. This electronic redistribution enhanced the Lewis acidity of Ce3+, reduced the nucleophilicity of PO₄3−, and enriched Ru sites with electrons, facilitating O₂ activation. Under anaerobic conditions, a distinct CO absorption peak appeared from 200 °C (Fig. 12c), attributed to the oxidation of intermediates by lattice oxygen from RuOₓ nanoclusters. In an oxygen atmosphere, CO signals were detectable from 50 °C, and the features of H₂O (3630–3260 cm−1, 1610 cm−1) and COₓ intensified with temperature (Fig. 12d), confirming Ru's role in enabling complete oxidation (including Ru0/CePO4 and RuOx/CePO4 sites). The suppression of VC over 1% Ru/CePO₄ (Fig. 7c) is attributed to a concerted mechanism: (1) Ru loading lowered the activation energy for CCl bond cleavage (Fig. 12f); (2) the electron transfer from CePO₄ to Ru weakened the β-H abstraction capability of PO₄3−; (3) reactive oxygen species generated at Ru0/RuOₓ sites rapidly oxidized the *CH₂CH₂Cl intermediate to COₓ/H₂O, preempting the VC-forming step. Consequently, DCE degradation over 1% Ru/CePO₄ proceeds via both L-H and MvK mechanisms. Notably, under O₂, the broad adsorbed H₂O band intensified above 250 °C for both catalysts, and the Ce–OH stretching vibration recovered above 300 °C (Fig. 12b,d), indicating water molecule dissociation on L acid sites. This competitive adsorption between H₂O and reactants explains the activity decline observed under humid conditions for 1% Ru/CePO4 (Fig. 9a,b).

For the 15% Zr/CePO₄ catalyst under anaerobic conditions (Fig. 13a), a weak =CH stretching vibration at 3030 cm−1 between 50 and 150 °C indicated the formation of adsorbed VC. This was accompanied by CCl vibrations from dissociated DCE (723, 684 cm−1) and a distinct CCl stretch at 779 cm−1 assigned to adsorbed VC, the intensity of which increased with temperature (Fig. S21). Above 200 °C, this adsorbed VC underwent further transformation via hydrolysis, evidenced by a C=C shoulder peak at 1634 cm−1 (enol intermediate), which tautomerized to acetaldehyde (ν(C=O) at 1667 cm−1; δ(CH₃) at 1380 cm−1) and was subsequently oxidized to acetate species (ν(C=O) at 1712 cm−1; ν(COO−) at 1582 cm−1; δ(CH₃) at 1380 cm−1) [50–52]. This “VC → enol → acetaldehyde → acetate” pathway under inert atmosphere was mediated by surface hydroxyl groups and lattice oxygen from ZrOₓ. In an O₂ atmosphere (Fig. 13b), the acetate features (ν(COO−) at 1582/1458 cm−1; δ(CH₃) at 1381/1361 cm−1) became more pronounced, as O₂ activated at ZrOₓ oxygen vacancies promoted deep oxidation. This mechanism, driven by the abundant acid-base sites (e.g., Zr4+, ZrOH, ZrO) on ZrOₓ, explains the higher VC yield observed during catalytic tests (Fig. 7c). Strikingly, the reaction landscape changed completely for the 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ composite. No characteristic VC signals were detected at low temperatures (Fig. 13c). The CCl stretching vibrations (682, 726 cm−1) diminished and vanished quickly with heating (Fig. S21), indicating accelerated chlorine removal. Notably, above 150 °C, vibrational bands associated with dehydrogenation oxidation products (carboxylates and carbonates) increased significantly (Fig. 13c). Under O₂ (Fig. 13d), only weak residual carboxylate features (νₐₛ(COO−) at 1582 cm−1) and diminishing water bands were observed, with no other intermediates detectable, pointing to the rapid and complete decomposition of all surface species. This behavior aligned with that of 1% Ru/ZrO₂ (Fig. S23). These results demonstrate that Ru incorporation into the ZrOₓ/CePO₄ system is transformative: it dramatically enhances lattice oxygen mobility and oxygen vacancy formation at the RuOₓ–ZrOₓ interface. This empowers the catalyst to activate and oxidize VC at low temperatures and to promote the deep oxidation of DCE dissociation products from neighboring interfaces (CePO₄ or ZrOₓ/CePO₄ interfaces) before they can desorb as harmful byproducts. Furthermore, the noticeable decrease in water vibration bands (3630–3260 cm−1, 1610 cm−1) with temperature for both Zr-containing catalysts (Fig. 13b,d) confirms the superior water tolerance imparted by the ZrOₓ (or RuOx-ZrOx) phase. This property enabled the efficient activation and conversion of water molecules, thereby facilitating the hydrolytic oxidation of DCE and VC, and preventing the formation of poly-chlorinated by-products.

Therefore, for 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄, the excellent performance and effective suppression of VC and polychlorinated by-products were governed by three defense lines orchestrated by its synergistic multiphase interfaces (Fig. 14 ): The unique acid–base pair (Ce3+–PO₄3−) on CePO₄ promoted rapid chlorine desorption as HCl, preventing surface chlorine accumulation and blocking deep chlorination pathways. The inherently weak redox properties of CePO₄ suppressed the Deacon reaction, thereby eliminating the in-situ generation of Cl₂, a key chlorinating agent for polychlorinated by-product formation. Together with the loaded Ru and ZrOₓ species, multifunctional interfaces were constructed. DCE first underwent efficient dehydrochlorination mainly at the acid–base sites of CePO₄ or the more acidic ZrOₓ/CePO₄ interfaces. The resulting VC intermediate was not released but was rapidly captured and removed through low-temperature oxidation and hydrolysis at neighboring RuOₓ–ZrOₓ/CePO₄ interfaces. Moreover, electronic interactions at the Ru0/CePO₄ and RuOₓ/CePO₄ interfaces facilitated CCl bond cleavage while simultaneously inhibiting the β-H elimination step critical for VC formation. The electron-enriched Ru sites enhanced lattice‑oxygen mobility and activated molecular oxygen via both Mars–van Krevelen and Langmuir–Hinshelwood pathways, ensuring deep oxidation of the dechlorinated intermediates (such as *CH₂CH₂Cl).

In this work, a multifunctional 1% Ru–15% Zr/CePO₄ catalyst was successfully synthesized via sequential impregnation. The catalyst demonstrates outstanding performance in the catalytic oxidation of 1,2-dichloroethane (DCE), featuring high activity (T₉₀ = 260 °C), remarkable long-term stability, excellent water tolerance, and—most notably—effective suppression of both vinyl chloride (VC) and polychlorinated by-products. This superior behavior originates from the rational design and synergistic interplay among multiple interfacial structures (CePO₄, ZrOₓ/CePO₄, Ru0/CePO₄, RuOₓ/CePO₄, and RuOₓ–ZrOₓ/CePO₄). This multi-interface synergy establishes an efficient and environmentally benign catalytic framework for the complete elimination of DCE or other CVOCs, offering a promising strategy to minimize secondary pollution from chlorinated byproducts.
